text.text: A narrower slab does not increase the prior probability of inclusion; instead, it concentrates the alternative model's prior mass on modest nonzero differences and can therefore give the observed data a higher marginal likelihood than a diffuse slab that also assigns mass to unsupported large differences.
This may initially seem counterintuitive because a narrower slab also shrinks an included difference more strongly toward zero.
However, the posterior magnitude of a difference conditional on inclusion and the evidence for inclusion are distinct quantities.

A narrower slab can produce a smaller posterior estimate while yielding a larger inclusion Bayes factor when its concentration on modest nonzero differences makes the observed data more probable under the alternative model.

In the limiting case where the slab scale approaches zero, the alternative becomes indistinguishable from the point null and BF10 approaches 1, so the relationship need not remain monotonic outside the examined range.
The Bayes factor falls below the descriptive threshold of 3 at a scale of approximately 0.92.
The shaded band represents Monte Carlo uncertainty in the estimated Bayes-factor curve, rather than posterior uncertainty about the edge parameter.
This result illustrates why a borderline Bayes factor should be interpreted together with a substantively defensible slab and a sensitivity analysis.
Across all 15 interaction differences, 12 retain the same classification throughout the scale range.
Table 3 lists the three exceptions.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref> lists the three exceptions.

text.text: At scale 0.5, three edges exceed BF10 = 3; at the default scale, 13 support equality and two are inconclusive; at scale 2, 14 support equality and one is inconclusive.
The sensitivity is therefore concentrated in a small number of borderline comparisons, but it is substantively important for the withdrawal-conflict edge selected for illustration.
Sampling diagnostics establish whether the posterior computation is sufficiently stable, but they do not establish whether the ordinal MRF adequately represents the observed data.
We therefore performed posterior predictive checks targeting aspects of the joint distribution that are not simply the marginal category frequencies.
We do not focus on marginal-frequency checks because the OMRF models the category structure of every variable flexibly, with a separate threshold parameter for each non-reference category.

Reproducing the observed marginals would consequently provide only a weak check of model adequacy; the more informative question is whether the fitted model reproduces associations and joint response patterns across variables.
For each of 500 draws from the joint posterior, we simulated a new dataset for women and men with the original group sizes.

We then calculated all 15 pairwise Spearman correlations, the proportion of participants rating both symptoms in each pair as "Often" or higher, and the distribution of the number of symptoms rated "Often" or higher.
The complete numerical summaries are available in the reproducibility archive.
Figure 8 compares the observed statistics with their posterior predictive distributions.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">8</ref> compares the observed statistics with their posterior predictive distributions.

text.text: An isolated observation outside a 95% posterior predictive interval is not by itself a definitive rejection of the model.
We regard multiple deviations in the same direction, or a clear deviation for a substantively central statistic, as evidence of potentially problematic fit.
All 30 group-specific Spearman correlations fall inside their 95% posterior predictive intervals, indicating that the model reproduces the overall rank-order associations reasonably well.
The upper-tail checks are less favorable: 9 of 15 observed co-occurrence proportions among women and all 15 among men exceed their 95% posterior predictive intervals.

The model also predicts too many participants with zero or one highly rated symptom and too few participants with several highly rated symptoms; five of the seven symptom-burden proportions among women and four among men fall outside their intervals.
Thus, the fitted ordinal MRF captures the broad pairwise association pattern but understates the clustering of high symptom responses.
These discrepancies do not directly demonstrate that the estimated edge differences are incorrect.

The adequate reproduction of the pairwise rank correlations provides some reassurance that the model captures broad pairwise association patterns relevant to the comparison, although these correlations are not themselves conditional edge parameters.

Nevertheless, the upper-tail results indicate additional dependence that the pairwise ordinal MRF does not represent, potentially because of higher-order interactions, latent heterogeneity, or another form of tail dependence.

Because this discrepancy is more pervasive among men, the omitted structure cannot simply be assumed to affect both groups identically and could be absorbed differently into their estimated edge parameters.
The inclusion Bayes factors therefore quantify evidence about equality of the groups' edge parameters within the fitted ordinal MRF approximation.
They do not establish equality of the complete joint symptom distributions or of the dependence structure among participants reporting multiple highly rated symptoms.

For the default scale of 1, the middle 50% of the prior lies between -0.67 and 0.67, and 95% lies between -1.96 and 1.96.
For an average interaction σij , the corresponding adjacent-category odds ratio is exp(2σ ij ).
The default middle 50% interval therefore corresponds to odds ratios from 0.26 to 3.85, while the 95% interval corresponds to 0.02 to 50.4.
This makes clear that the default is broad on the odds-ratio scale even though a scale of 1 may appear modest numerically.
The same parameter interval has a different substantive translation for the two types of group differences.
For an interaction difference δ ij , exp(2δ ij ) is the ratio of the adjacent-category odds ratios in Group 2 and Group 1.
For a threshold difference δ ih , exp(δ ih ) is the ratio of the corresponding baseline category odds.
Thus, under the default Normal prior, the 95% interval implies a prior interaction-odds-ratio ratio from 0.02 to 50.4 and a prior baseline-odds ratio from 0.14 to 7.10.

A scale of 0.5 may be preferable when theory or previous studies suggest that conditional associations and group differences are modest: its 95% interval for an interaction translates to odds ratios from 0.14 to 7.10.
A scale of 2 is very permissive; its 95% interval translates to interaction odds ratios from approximately 0.0004 to 2,540.
Such a dispersed choice should generally be motivated by credible evidence that very large parameters are possible.
For model selection, the scale is consequential: a wider slab spreads prior mass across a larger range and can reduce the Bayes factor for a modest observed difference.
Applied analyses should therefore report the scale and examine whether conclusions near an evidential cutoff are stable under plausible alternatives.
